settings.subtitle: Your shot sent your hair a famine signal. A huge batch of follicles stopped growing at the same time. Here's why biotin can't restart them, and the molecule that keeps them growing. No DHT blocker. No quitting the shot.

You finally like the woman in the mirror.

Then you step out of the shower and look down at the drain.

That's not a few hairs. That's a nest. You pull it out with 2 fingers and it keeps coming. Your brush is full again. There are strands on your pillow, on your shoulders, and on the back of your chair. Your ponytail used to fill your hand. Now it wraps around an extra time.

And your part. Was it always this wide?

You did everything right. You lost the weight. You hit your protein. Your labs came back normal. And your doctor shrugged: "It's just the weight loss. Take some biotin."

So you took the biotin. You stirred collagen into your coffee. Maybe you tried the pumpkin seed pills the ads keep showing you.

The drain didn't care.

settings.paragraph_text:
The hair falling out today stopped growing about 3 months ago.

When your shot cut your appetite, your body read it as a famine. In a famine, your body shuts down whatever it doesn't need to stay alive. Your hair is first in line. The cells at the root of each hair are some of the fastest-dividing cells you have. They're expensive to run.

So your body flipped a switch. A huge batch of follicles left the growth phase at the same time and went to rest. Doctors have a name for it: telogen effluvium. I call it the Famine Shed.

A resting hair doesn't fall right away. It sits in your scalp for 2 to 3 months. Then it lets go. That's why it seemed to come out of nowhere around month 3, 4, or 5. By the time you saw the first clump, the switch had already flipped.

That's why biotin "didn't work." Biotin is a building material. Your follicles weren't short on bricks. They were shut down. You can stack bricks outside a closed factory all year. Nothing gets built until somebody turns the machines back on.

That's why the DHT blockers miss too. DHT is the hormone behind pattern baldness. Your hair didn't go in a pattern. It let go all over your head, all at once.

settings.paragraph_text:
So the question was never "What is my hair missing?" The real question is "How do I keep my follicles in the growth phase while I'm still eating less?"

Because you are not quitting the shot. You shouldn't have to pick between the body you worked for and the hair you've always had.

It's called spermidine. Every cell in your body makes it. You eat it in wheat germ, aged cheese, and mushrooms. When you fast, your body raises its own levels. It's the molecule your body reaches for in lean times.

Your hair roots need it. Spermidine is the only raw material your cells can use to switch on eIF5A, a protein that fast-dividing cells need to keep building.

In a 90-day, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 100 adults, a spermidine-based supplement raised the share of hairs in the active growth phase by 52%. On placebo, it dropped 21%.

6 months in, right through autumn shedding season, the researchers gave each person's hair a firm tug. In the spermidine group, it came out loose in 0% of people. On placebo: 68%.

The Famine Shed runs on a delay. That works against you, and it can work for you.

Every week you're on the shot and eating less, the famine signal keeps firing. Every week it fires, more follicles go to rest. Every follicle that goes to rest today falls out 2 to 3 months from now.

Weak growth signal means more follicles at rest. More follicles at rest means more hair in the drain in 3 months. A strong growth signal means more follicles stay growing. More follicles growing means a fuller ponytail in 3 months.

settings.question: Biotin didn't work for me. Why would this?
settings.answer: Biotin only fixes a biotin shortfall. Your labs were probably normal. Your follicles weren't short on materials. They were switched to rest. Spermidine was tested on exactly that: how many hairs stay in the growth phase.

settings.question: Won't my hair just grow back on its own?
settings.answer: A lot of it will, eventually. Full thickness takes 12 to 18 months. And as long as you're on the shot and eating less, the famine signal keeps firing. That's why so many women get a 2nd wave. [BRAND] works on keeping follicles growing while the trigger is still there.

settings.question: Do I have to quit the shot?
settings.answer: No. Many women quit and keep shedding anyway, because the hairs that fell were switched to rest months earlier. Quitting doesn't flip them back. Keep the shot. Keep the weight off. Give your follicles the growth signal.

settings.question: Why not minoxidil?
settings.answer: It works for some women. It also means a prescription or a greasy scalp, a "dread shed" when you start, and a habit for good. [BRAND] works on a different lever: it keeps the follicle in the growth phase, with no dread shed.

settings.question: Isn't this just another vitamin?
settings.answer: No. Spermidine is a polyamine, a molecule every cell makes. It's the only raw material your cells can use to switch on eIF5A. No vitamin does that.

settings.question: Is my hair loss permanent?
settings.answer: Most GLP-1 shedding is telogen effluvium. That's the Famine Shed, and it's temporary. A smaller group, mostly people with a family history, see pattern hair loss show up. That's a hormone problem, and it's a different conversation.

settings.question: How soon will I see a difference?
settings.answer: Hair runs on a 3-month clock. Hairs already at rest when you start will still fall in the first weeks. The trial measured at 90 days and again at 6 months. Give it 3 months.

settings.question: Does it work for men?
settings.answer: Yes. The trial had more men than women. Men on a GLP-1 get the Famine Shed far less often. If your loss is at the temples or crown, that's more likely pattern loss.
